query: High-entropy alloys can combine mechanical strength, wear resistance, corrosion protection, oxidation resistance, and thermal stability, while their large compositional space offers opportunities to tune degradation in harsh environments. Prior studies have largely considered wear and corrosion separately, and only a few reports address their combined action, leaving the governing behavior poorly understood. For a high-entropy alloy subjected to tribo-corrosion, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs the coupled response and why? Describe a controlled comparison that would isolate the governing cause, predict changes in total degradation and its wear and corrosion components relative to a matched baseline, state where the prediction should hold or fail, connect it to the available prior evidence, and identify a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Under tribo-corrosion conditions, the wear-induced formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline surface layer in high-entropy alloys promotes rapid passivation that simultaneously moderates both mechanical wear and corrosion. This dynamic surface refinement is the single mechanistic mediator that couples the responses: it reduces localized corrosion by accelerating the oxide film formation while also modifying the wear behavior.
generation.material_initial_state: A coarse- or moderately-grained single-phase high-entropy alloy (e.g., CoCrFeMnNi) before sliding.
generation.intervention: Subject the alloy to controlled sliding/contact in a corrosive environment (e.g., neutral/alkaline electrolyte with dissolved oxygen) versus an inert environment.
generation.conditions: Testing performed under controlled tribological contact at identical loads and speeds. One test in an electrochemically active environment (allowing passivation) and a matched baseline test in an inert medium where corrosion processes are minimal.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline, dynamically amorphized near-surface layer induced by wear.
generation.mechanism: The mechanically induced grain refinement accelerates the formation of a protective oxide/passivation film by increasing the surface area and reactive sites. This passivating film in turn slows corrosion, while the evolved microstructure also changes the wear response. Together, the coupled processes lead to a net degradation that is lower than expected if wear and corrosion acted independently.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to a baseline specimen without significant wear-induced surface refinement, the alloy under tribo-corrosion would exhibit a lower or controlled total degradation. Specifically, the corrosion component is reduced due to accelerated passivation, even if the wear rate shows its own characteristic behavior. In an inert environment, the wear rate would be low (as seen in prior inert tests) without the added effect of passivation.
generation.baseline: Tribological testing in an inert environment where oxidation and mixed metal-oxide films are mitigated, corresponding to the conditions reported with low friction and wear in previous studies.
generation.boundary: The prediction holds when the environment supports rapid passivation (i.e., readily forming a stable oxide film). The mechanism may fail or be less pronounced in highly aggressive electrolytes (for instance, those saturated with chlorides) where passivation is inhibited or when the sliding conditions do not induce sufficient dynamic amorphization.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative extent to which passivation reduces the corrosion component relative to the wear component is uncertain, as is the specific nature of the nano-structured film over extended durations. The interaction between mechanical deformation and passivation kinetics in harsh environments requires further characterization.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare identical high-entropy alloy samples and subject them to sliding wear tests under two conditions: one in a corrosive electrolyte that facilitates oxide passivation and one in an inert atmosphere. Monitor the evolution of the near-surface microstructure using techniques like STEM or XRD, and measure both wear rates (via profilometry or mass loss) and corrosion rates (via electrochemical impedance spectroscopy and potentiodynamic polarization).
measurements: Surface grain size and phase characterization before and after sliding
Surface oxide film composition and thickness
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the wear-induced surface layer is not significantly refined (i.e., lacks ultra-nanocrystalline features) in the corrosive environment, or if the corrosion rate does not decrease (or even increases) relative to the baseline inert test despite similar wear, then the hypothesis that the dynamically induced nano-layer mediates both wear and corrosion via accelerated passivation is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
Evidence of Inverse Hall-Petch Behavior and Low Friction and Wear in High Entropy Alloys

Abstract: AbstractWe present evidence of inverse Hall-Petch behavior for a single-phase high entropy alloy (CoCrFeMnNi) in ultra-high vacuum and show that it is associated with low friction coefficients (~0.3). Grain size measurements by STEM validate a recently proposed dynamic amorphization model that accurately predicts grain size-dependent shear strength in the inverse Hall-Petch regime. Wear rates in the initially soft (coarse grained) material were shown to be remarkably low (~10–6 mm3/N-m), the lowest for any HEA tested in an inert environment where oxidation and the formation of mixed metal-oxide films is mitigated. The combined high wear resistance and low friction are linked to the formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer. The dynamic amorphization model was also used to predict an average high angle grain boundary energy (0.87 J/m2). This value was used to explain cavitation-induced nanoporosity found in the highly deformed surface layer, a phenomenon that has been linked to superplasticity.Subject terms: Structural materials, Structural properties
